ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, a quarter-circular vertical track $AB$ with a radius of $2\mathrm{m}$ is connected to an inclined straight track $BC$. A small ball with a mass of $0.2\mathrm{kg}$ is released from point $A$. When it passes point $B$ on the circular track, a sensor measures the normal force exerted by the track to be $3.6\mathrm{N}$. The ball then flies horizontally and lands exactly at the end point $C$ of the straight track. The vertical height difference between points $B$ and $C$ is $3.2\mathrm{m}$. Neglecting air resistance and taking the gravitational acceleration $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, find:

1. What is the magnitude of the velocity of the small ball when it reaches point $B$?
2. What is the horizontal distance between points $B$ and $C$?
3. How long after the small ball flies out from point $B$ does it reach the farthest distance from the straight track $BC$?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the upper left of the figure is a quarter-circular arc track AB; the small ball goes from A along the circular arc to the lower right end B; at point B, the radius direction of the circular arc is vertically upward, so the tangent direction is horizontal. At the lower right of point B there is an inclined straight track BC, with C on the ground; from B to C there is also a dashed parabola drawn, indicating that the small ball, after flying out horizontally from B, lands at C. The figure marks the vertical height from B to the ground as h = 3.2 m. Reasoning: 1. At point B, the radial direction toward the center of the circle is vertically upward. According to the specified method, the normal force N is upward and gravity mg is downward, providing the centripetal force: N - mg = m v_B^2 / R. Substituting N = 3.6 N, m = 0.2 kg, g = 10 m/s^2, R = 2 m, gives 3.6 - 0.2*10 = 0.2*v_B^2/2, that is, 1.6 = 0.1 v_B^2, so v_B^2 = 16, v_B = 4 m/s. 2. The small ball is thrown horizontally from B, and the vertical falling height is h = 3.2 m. In the vertical direction: h = (1/2) g t_C^2, so 3.2 = 5 t_C^2, t_C^2 = 0.64, t_C = 0.8 s. In the horizontal direction it is uniform motion: x_C = v_B t_C = 4*0.8 = 3.2 m. Therefore the horizontal distance between B and C is 3.2 m. 3. Take B as the origin, with x to the right and y downward. The projectile motion equations are x = 4t, y = (1/2)gt^2 = 5t^2. The coordinates of C are (3.2, 3.2), therefore the straight line on which straight track BC lies is y = (3.2/3.2)x = x. The distance from the small ball to the straight line BC is proportional to numerator = x - y = 4t - 5t^2, because the denominator sqrt(1^2+1) is a constant. Find the maximum value of 4t - 5t^2: d/dt(4t - 5t^2) = 4 - 10t = 0, giving t = 0.4 s, and it is between 0 and 0.8 s, so the distance is greatest at this time. Final answer: v_B = 4 m/s; horizontal distance between B and C = 3.2 m; 0.4 s after flying out of B, the distance from the straight track BC is the greatest.
